why.Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest cou: When arriving on the Watson, Blum and Bacon traverse, since that party is already on the Bacon side and reaches the saddle from there instead of dropping back to the Blum Lakes basin.

review.notes: Blum Lakes approach is the documented one for a stand-alone climb; the saddle line fits traverse parties.

why.Buck Creek Pass and the grass slopes: When already camped at Buck Creek Pass on a backpacking trip, trading the break-off boot path for a steeper direct climb; only on dry ground, as wet grass and heather turn dangerous.

review.notes: Recent reports leave the trail at the climbers' path to Pass No Pass; the pass line is the other documented option.

why.The short way: the border swath from the: When the lake and ranger station can be reached by boat or the northern road, and a party accepts hours of steep, overgrown brush to save the miles of the long ridge trail.

review.notes: Climbing-club route page starts at the ranger station and also lists the ridge trail; the practicality of the long trail is stored research.
fromStoredNotes: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station

problems: Mountaineers route page lists the ranger-station swath start, which conflicts with the primary mark of the ridge trail; evidence on which is most used is mixed. Mark left unchanged.

why.Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through He: When spending the night, because camping at Lake Ingalls is not allowed and the basin has legal sites and water; day parties skip the extra drop and climb.

review.notes: Trail split just past the pass; the alternate drops into the basin and rejoins below the lake.

why.Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then: To avoid the steep, blowdown-choked lower Lake Constance climbers' trail, for parties willing to trade about eight extra miles and a two or three day trip for easier tread.

review.notes: Search found Constance Pass trail and Crystal Pass geography but nothing on Inner Constance itself; reason drawn from the stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass

problems: Variant 0 notes mention the South Gully and the Thumb, which are Mount Constance features; possible cross-peak contamination.
Stored prose calls the Lake Constance line more commonly used, matching the primary mark.

why.Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern s: When the boat service is running, usually from about early June, and a party wants to skip the trail miles and accepts a booked pickup time.
why.Before the highway opens: the gate at mi: In late winter or early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow; the road to the trailhead is covered by bike or skis first.

review.notes: Reports confirm taxi not before early June and not in winter; closed-gate bike or ski approach is used in winter.

why.East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek: When the water taxi is not running or booked, such as before early June, or a party prefers not to depend on a pickup; costs several hours of flat walking each way.

review.notes: A north ridge trip report used the water taxi to May Creek; the trail is the fallback.

why.Two camps at the end of the same approac: For parties wanting the meadow camp, which keeps running water later in the season and puts summit day on the right side of the notch, at the cost of a descent and re-ascent.

review.notes: Trip reports describe camping both at Jerry Lakes and in the Crater Creek meadow.

why.Two camps at the end of the same approac: For parties wanting the meadow camp, which holds running water later in the season and starts summit day beneath the shoulder where the ridge is gained, after a descent and re-ascent.

review.notes: Same shared approach and camp choice as the South Face.

why.White River trail from the east: When approaching from the Lake Wenatchee side, or when the Sauk valley is unavailable; about as far on foot but with less trail and more cross-country travel.

review.notes: The Sauk and White Pass line is the well documented standard; White River is similar in length with less trail.

why.Columbia Glacier from the Blanca Lake ba: When the glacier is snow-covered and firm enough to travel, often as the other half of a loop with the ridge path; early season it is the safer choice when the ridge is snowy.

review.notes: Reports describe the south ridge from Virgin Lake and a glacier variation from the Blanca basin.

why.Slate Pass and the Pasayten side: When starting high from the Harts Pass road to avoid the long Monument Creek valley, accepting longer, more cross-country travel and tread that is harder to follow.

review.notes: Pistol Pass is the usual line; Slate Pass start is documented as an alternative.

problems: Primary notes call the Eureka Creek crossing an unbridged ford, but a new trail bridge was reportedly built in 2022; that note may be out of date.
